n: The book opens with a title linking it to Solomon, David’s son, famed for the wisdom God gave him. The book itself shows later collections were added (Hezekiah’s scribes, Agur, Lemuel), so “Solomon” heads the whole anthology.

f.g: Hebrew mashal—a short saying, comparison, or parable that packs truth into a memorable line.

n: Verses 2–6 state the book’s purpose. It is meant to help readers gain wisdom (skill for living well), accept correction, and understand wise teaching.

f.g: Hebrew ḥokmah—practical skill in living, the know-how of a craftsman applied to life and righteousness.
Hebrew musar—discipline, training, or correction, like a parent shaping a child.

n: Wisdom here isn’t just cleverness. It includes moral qualities: doing what is right, fair, and honest toward others.

f.g: equity = fairness, uprightness; treating people evenly.

n: Proverbs is especially written for the inexperienced and the young, to give them good sense before life tests them.

f.g: subtilty = shrewdness, prudence—here a good quality: the ability to see through traps.
The naive or inexperienced—someone easily led, not yet set in either wisdom or folly.

n: Proverbs is not only for beginners. Even the wise grow wiser by listening, and those who understand can gain skill in guiding their lives.

f.g: Literally “steering”—the skill of a sailor guiding a ship.

n: The book will teach how to understand proverbs, riddles, and deep sayings. Wisdom literature often makes the reader think hard to unlock its meaning.

f.g: dark sayings = riddles or puzzling sayings that need thought to understand.

n: This is the motto of the whole book. True knowledge begins with reverence for the Lord. Refusing that foundation is what makes someone a “fool” in Proverbs—a moral, not mental, failure.

f.g: Reverent awe, trust, and obedience toward Jehovah.
Hebrew ʾevil—a person who is morally stubborn and refuses correction, not merely unintelligent.

n: The first lecture begins. A father addresses his son, but both parents teach. In Israel, family instruction was the first school of faith.

f.g: A teacher’s affectionate address to a student or child; it appears often in Proverbs 1–7.

n: Parents’ teachings are like a lovely garland on the head and a necklace—something that adorns and honors the one who wears it.

f.g: A graceful wreath or garland worn on the head.

n: A short, firm warning: when sinners try to lure you in, just say no. The rest of the passage shows how persuasive such invitations can be.

f.g: entice = lure, persuade with tempting promises.

n: The father quotes the gang’s pitch: let’s ambush someone innocent just because we can. The violence is planned and unprovoked.

f.g: privily = secretly; to hide and wait in ambush.

n: The gang brags they will swallow their victims whole, like the grave (Sheol) swallows the dead. They imagine themselves as powerful as death itself.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the realm of the dead.
Another name for the grave or the world of the dead.

n: Their real motive is greed: easy riches and houses full of loot. Crime is sold as a shortcut to wealth.

f.g: spoil = plunder, loot taken by force.

n: The final hook is belonging: join us, share our common fund. Peer pressure offers friendship and equal shares.

f.w: Cast in thy lot among us
f.g: Throw in with us; join our group and share its fortunes.

n: The father’s answer: don’t even start down that road with them. Avoiding the first step is the surest protection.

f.w: refrain thy foot from their path

n: Their feet are fast to do harm. Isaiah used nearly the same words, and Paul quoted them to describe human sinfulness.

A puzzling proverb. One likely meaning: a bird that sees the net being spread will avoid it—so you, warned in advance, should avoid this trap. Another reading: even birds aren’t that foolish, yet these men are.

f.w: in vain the net is spread
f.g: A fowler’s net was useless if the bird watched it being set.

n: The irony: the ambush they set for others is really an ambush for themselves. Violence destroys the violent.

f.w: they lay wait for their own blood

n: The lesson of the story: greed for dishonest gain ends up taking the life of the very person who grasps it.
A new speaker appears: Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman preaching in public. Unlike the gang lurking in secret, Wisdom speaks openly to everyone.

f.g: without = outside, in public places.

n: She goes where crowds gather—the busiest streets and the city gates, where business and court cases took place. Wisdom is available to anyone who will listen.

f.g: The noisiest, busiest spot where people crowd together.
City gates were the ancient town square, where elders judged cases.

n: Wisdom asks three kinds of people “how long?”: the naive who enjoy being naive, mockers who love to mock, and fools who hate knowledge.

f.g: scorners = mockers, scoffers who ridicule correction and holy things.

n: Wisdom’s invitation: turn around when I correct you, and I will pour out my spirit and teach you. Repentance opens the door to revelation.

f.w: I will pour out my spirit unto you

f.g: reproof = correction, rebuke.

n: Wisdom has called repeatedly and held out her hand like someone beckoning, but no one paid attention.

f.w: I have stretched out my hand

n: They treated her advice as worthless and wanted none of her correction.

f.g: set at nought = treated as nothing, disregarded.

n: Strong poetic language: when disaster comes, Wisdom will “laugh.” The point is not cruelty but that those who mocked wisdom will find their mockery turned back on them.

f.w: I also will laugh at your calamity

n: Disaster is pictured as a sudden storm or whirlwind. The consequences of ignoring wisdom often arrive all at once.
In crisis they finally call, but too late. The warning is that refusing wisdom over and over can leave a person without it when they need it most.

f.g: early = eagerly, diligently.

n: The reason is clear: they chose this. They hated knowledge and refused to reverence the Lord. Wisdom respects human agency.

f.w: did not choose the fear of the LORD

n: A summary restatement: they wanted none of Wisdom’s counsel and despised her correction.

f.w: They would none of my counsel

n: The principle of natural consequences: they will eat the fruit of the path they chose. People are “filled” with their own schemes.

f.w: eat of the fruit of their own way

f.g: devices = schemes, plans.

n: Wandering from wisdom kills the naive, and the careless ease of fools ruins them. Comfort without wisdom can be deadly.

f.g: Their careless ease or complacency.

n: The chapter ends with a promise: whoever listens to Wisdom will live securely and be at peace, free from dread.
